We need to produce a resume for Matthias Algiers. Use words with all capital letters to highlight key abilities, but ensure that words with all capital letters appear less than 10 times. So we can use maybe 5 or fewer capitalized words. Wrap entire response with double quotation marks. That means the output should start with a double quote and end with a double quote, and everything inside is the resume.

We need to be careful not to accidentally include other capitalized words like proper nouns (Matthias, Algiers) - those are capitalized but not all caps. The requirement: "words with all capital letters" means words that are fully uppercase, like "LEADER", "MANAGER". Those count towards the limit (<10). So we need to limit those to less than 10 occurrences. We can use maybe 3-5 uppercase words for key abilities.

We must ensure not to inadvertently have uppercase words like "I" (single letter) counts as all caps? "I" is a single letter uppercase, but it's a word. Does that count? Probably yes, as it's all caps. Safer to avoid using "I" as a separate word; we can write in third person or avoid "I". Use "Matthias" as subject, avoid "I". Also avoid "A" as uppercase single letter. So we should avoid single-letter words that are uppercase. Use lowercase for articles, etc. So we need to watch out.

We can write resume in paragraphs, using bullet points maybe with hyphens. Ensure no unintended all-caps words. Use capitalized words for key abilities like "LEADERSHIP", "STRATEGIC THINKING", "PROJECT MANAGEMENT", "DATA ANALYSIS", "COMMUNICATION". Those are all caps and count. We need less than 10 occurrences. If we use each once, that's 5. Good.

We must ensure not to accidentally repeat them more than needed. Also avoid other all caps like "USA", "UK", "CEO", etc. Those are also all caps and would count. So avoid those. Also avoid acronyms like "SQL", "HTML". Those are all caps and would count. Better to avoid them or use lowercase versions. But we could use them if we keep count under 10. Safer to avoid.

Thus produce resume with maybe:

"Matthias Algiers
[Contact info]
PROFESSIONAL SUMMARY
... (no all caps)
KEY ABILITIES: LEADERSHIP, STRATEGIC THINKING, PROJECT MANAGEMENT, DATA ANALYSIS, COMMUNICATION
PROFESSIONAL EXPERIENCE
...
EDUCATION
...
SKILLS
..."

We need to ensure that the all caps words appear less than 10 times. In the line "KEY ABILITIES: LEADERSHIP, STRATEGIC THINKING, PROJECT MANAGEMENT, DATA ANALYSIS, COMMUNICATION" we have each ability as separate word? Actually "LEADERSHIP" is one word, "STRATEGIC" and "THINKING" are two words, both uppercase. "PROJECT" and "MANAGEMENT" two words. "DATA" and "ANALYSIS" two words. "COMMUNICATION" one word. So total uppercase words: LEADERSHIP (1), STRATEGIC (2), THINKING (3), PROJECT (4), MANAGEMENT (5), DATA (6), ANALYSIS (7), COMMUNICATION (8). That's 8 occurrences, less than 10. Good.

We must ensure not to accidentally have other uppercase words elsewhere like "Matthias" (capitalized but not all caps) okay. "Algiers" okay. "PROFESSIONAL" is all caps? If we write "PROFESSIONAL SUMMARY" that would be two uppercase words, adding to count. So we should avoid using all caps for section headings; we can use title case (first letter capital) or lowercase. Use normal capitalization: "Professional Summary", "Key Abilities", "Professional Experience", "Education", "Skills". Those are not all caps.

We must also avoid "USA", "UK", "LLC", etc.

We need to wrap entire response with double quotation marks. So output should start with a double quote, then the resume content, then ending double quote. Ensure no extra whitespace outside? Probably fine.

Let's craft resume:

"Matthias Algiers
Email: matthias.algiers@example.com | Phone: (555) 123-4567 | LinkedIn: linkedin.com/in/matthiasalgiers
Professional Summary
Dynamic professional with over 8 years of experience driving cross-functional initiatives, optimizing processes, and delivering measurable results. Adept at leading teams, analyzing complex data, and communicating insights to stakeholders.
Key Abilities: LEADERSHIP, STRATEGIC THINKING, PROJECT MANAGEMENT, DATA ANALYSIS, COMMUNICATION
Professional Experience
Senior Analyst, XYZ Corporation, Cityville, ST — March 2020 – Present
- Lead a team of five analysts to develop forecasting models that improved forecast accuracy by 15%
- Strategically plan and execute quarterly business reviews, aligning departmental goals with corporate objectives
- Manage end-to-end project lifecycles for process improvement initiatives, resulting in 10% cost reduction
- Conduct deep-dive data analysis using statistical tools to identify trends and recommend actionable strategies
- Communicate findings to executive leadership through clear presentations and reports
Analyst, ABC Industries, Townsburg, ST — June 2015 – February 2020
- Supported strategic planning efforts by analyzing market data and competitor performance
- Assisted project managers in tracking milestones, budgets, and resource allocation
- Performed data cleaning and visualization to support decision-making processes
- Communicated technical information to non-technical stakeholders in an accessible manner
Education
Master of Science in Business Analytics, University of State, Cityville, ST — 2015
Bachelor of Arts in Economics, State College, Townsburg, ST — 2012
Skills
- Leadership & Team Management
- Strategic Planning & Execution
- Project Coordination
- Data Analysis & Statistical Modeling
- Effective Communication & Presentation
- Problem Solving & Critical Thinking"

Now count uppercase words: We have "LEADERSHIP", "STRATEGIC", "THINKING", "PROJECT", "MANAGEMENT", "DATA", "ANALYSIS", "COMMUNICATION". That's 8. No other all caps. Check for any accidental all caps like "ST" (state abbreviation) appears multiple times: "ST" is all caps and counts as a word. That would increase count. We used "ST" in address lines: "Cityville, ST", "Townsburg, ST". That's two occurrences each? Actually each line has "ST". Let's see: "Senior Analyst, XYZ Corporation, Cityville, ST — March 2020 – Present" includes "ST". Also "Analyst, ABC Industries, Townsburg, ST — June 2015 – February 2020". Also "Master of Science in Business Analytics, University of State, Cityville, ST — 2015". Also "Bachelor of Arts in Economics, State College, Townsburg, ST — 2012". That's four occurrences of "ST". Each is an uppercase word, so that adds 4 more, making total 12, exceeding limit.

We need to avoid using "ST" as all caps. Could write "State" spelled out, or use lowercase "st"? But postal abbreviation is usually uppercase; we could write "State" instead. Or we could omit the state abbreviation entirely. Let's replace "ST" with "State". Or we could write "state" lowercase. Use "State". That will not be all caps.

Thus modify lines: "Cityville, State", "Townsburg, State". Also "University of State, Cityville, State". Actually "University of State" maybe redundant but okay. Or we could write "University of State, Cityville". Let's just write "Cityville, State". For brevity.

Also need to avoid other all caps like "USA". Not present.

Now check again for any other all caps: "XYZ" is all caps, appears in "XYZ Corporation". That's an uppercase word. Also "ABC" in "ABC Industries". Those count. So we have XYZ (1), ABC (2). Plus the abilities (8) = 10. Actually we need less than 10, so we need total <=9. Currently we have abilities 8 + XYZ + ABC = 10. That's equal to 10, but requirement is less than 10, so must be <=9. So we need to reduce either abilities count or remove XYZ/ABC or change them to not all caps.

We could change company names to normal case: "Xyz Corporation" (capital X only) or "Xyz Corp". But "Xyz" still has capital X only, not all caps. Or we could use "Xyz Corporation" (Xyz not all caps). Similarly "Abc Industries". That would remove those all caps.
